section.title: Against Corrupt Leaders and Prophets
section.sectionRationale: Micah turns to the three groups who should have safeguarded the nation: rulers, prophets, and priests. Instead they devour the people, preach for pay, and judge for bribes, all while leaning on the LORD and assuming they are safe. Against them Micah stands alone, filled with the Spirit, to declare their sin. The chapter climaxes in the most shocking sentence in the book: Zion itself, temple and all, will be plowed under.
section.thesis: Leaders who exploit the people they were meant to protect, and prophets who sell a false peace, provoke God's silence and His severest judgment; only the prophet filled with the Spirit of the LORD dares tell the truth, and the truth is that even the temple mount will be leveled.
section.frameNote: Three movements framed by the theme of justice: the rulers who cannibalize the people (1-4); the prophets who preach for profit, against whom stands the Spirit-filled Micah (5-8); and the verdict on the whole corrupt establishment, Zion plowed like a field (9-12).

verses.text: Then I said: “Hear now, O leaders of Jacob, you rulers of the house of Israel. Should you not know {{mishpat|justice}}?
You hate good and love evil. You tear the skin from my people and strip the flesh from their bones.
You eat the flesh of my people after stripping off their skin and breaking their bones. You chop them up like flesh for the cooking pot, like meat in a cauldron.”
Then they will cry out to the LORD, but He will not answer them. At that time He will hide His face from them because of the evil they have done.

units.label: Prophets for profit, and the Spirit-filled prophet
units.note: peace for those who feed them

verses.text: This is what the LORD says: “As for the prophets who lead My people astray, who proclaim peace while they chew with their teeth, but declare war against one who puts nothing in their mouths:
Therefore night will come over you without visions, and darkness without divination. The sun will set on these prophets, and the daylight will turn black over them.
Then the seers will be ashamed and the diviners will be disgraced. They will all cover their mouths because there is no answer from God.”
As for me, however, I am filled with power by the {{ruach|Spirit}} of the LORD, with justice and courage, to declare to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin.

units.label: Zion plowed like a field
units.note: the temple mount a wooded ridge

verses.text: Now hear this, O leaders of the house of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel, who despise justice and pervert all that is right,
who build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with iniquity.

Her leaders judge for a bribe, her priests teach for a price, and her prophets practice divination for money. Yet they lean upon the LORD, saying, “Is not the LORD among us? No disaster can come upon us.”
Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble, and the temple mount a wooded ridge.

mishpat.gloss: Justice, judgment, the right ordering of life according to God's will, especially the fair treatment of the weak. It is the very thing the leaders were charged to know and uphold, and the very thing they despise. In Micah mishpat is not a cold legal idea but the concrete protection of the vulnerable; to pervert it is to attack God's own character.

ruach.gloss: Breath, wind, spirit. Here the Spirit of the LORD fills Micah with power, justice, and courage to speak the truth that others sell or suppress. The same word for the empty windbag prophet, a man of wind in 2:11, stands in sharp contrast: false prophets are full of mere air, while the true prophet is filled with the Spirit of God.

basic.context: Micah confronts the three groups who held power in Judah: government leaders, prophets, and priests. All three had turned their calling into a racket. The rulers exploited the people so violently that Micah pictures it as cannibalism. The prophets preached peace to whoever fed them and threatened war on whoever did not. The priests taught only for a price. Worst of all, they all assumed God was on their side and that no disaster could touch them. Micah, alone and Spirit-filled, tells them the truth.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a judgment oracle against leaders, and its abiding lesson is that spiritual privilege without integrity invites God's severest judgment. The chapter is famous for verse 12, quoted a century later in Jeremiah 26, where the elders recall that Micah's warning led King Hezekiah to repent, so Jerusalem was spared in that generation. Prophecy warns in order to bring repentance, not merely to predict.
basic.originalLanguages: The key word is mishpat, justice, what the leaders should know but despise. Against the false prophets, described in 2:11 as men of wind, ruach, empty air, stands Micah, who is filled with the ruach, the Spirit, of the LORD, with power, justice, and courage. The same word points in two directions: hollow air in the false, the very breath of God in the true.
basic.typology: Micah, the lone Spirit-filled truth-teller standing against corrupt shepherds, foreshadows Christ, the true Prophet anointed by the Spirit, who confronted the religious leaders of His day and cleansed the temple. The failed shepherds who devour the flock set up the promise of the true Shepherd to come.
basic.christ: Jesus is everything these leaders were not. He is the Prophet full of the Spirit, the Shepherd who lays down His life instead of devouring the sheep, and the Priest who teaches and gives freely rather than for pay. He wept over the same Jerusalem Micah condemned and foretold its destruction again, and He is the true Temple, torn down and raised in three days.
basic.god: God cares intensely about justice, especially the protection of the weak, and He will not be bought or flattered. The leaders assumed His presence guaranteed their safety; instead His presence guaranteed their accountability. When leaders trade truth for money, God withdraws His answer, His silence itself a judgment.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 34 condemns shepherds who feed themselves instead of the flock. Jeremiah 26 recalls this very chapter and Hezekiah's repentance. Matthew 23 records Jesus confronting corrupt religious leaders, and John 2 shows Him cleansing the temple these men had defiled.
basic.oneStory: Micah 3 exposes the tragedy of leaders who use God's people for their own gain and presume on His favor. Their failure cries out for a different kind of leader: a Shepherd who serves rather than devours, a Prophet full of the Spirit, a Priest who gives freely. That leader is Jesus, and the temple leveled here is answered by the true Temple He builds, His own risen body and His people.

context.literary:
The chapter opens with a small hinge that is easy to miss: 'Then I said,' verse 1. Chapter 2 ended with the LORD's own promise to gather the remnant like sheep, and the prophet now turns on the human shepherds who should have been doing that gathering. The oracle falls into three panels, and the summons 'Hear' stands at the head of the first and the third, verses 1 and 9, binding the outer panels as a frame around the prophets in the middle.

Inside that frame the accusations run in a deliberate order. Verses 1 to 3 charge the rulers with a crime, verse 4 gives the sentence, verses 5 to 7 charge the prophets and sentence them, and verse 8 is the prophet's own testimony. Then verses 9 to 11 gather all three offices, rulers, priests and prophets, into one indictment, and verse 12 delivers a single sentence for the lot. Each panel pairs a sin with a mirror-image penalty. Those who devoured the people are not answered when they cry out, verse 4. Those who sold visions lose every vision, verses 6 and 7. Those who built the city on blood watch it become a field, verse 12.

The butchery picture of verses 2 and 3 is built as a descending list: skin, flesh, bones, the cooking pot. The leaders do not merely rob the poor; they process them. Verse 8 is the hinge, set against the grain of the chapter. Everywhere else in chapter 3 Micah says 'you'; only here does he say 'I', and only here does he claim a gift rather than make a charge.
context.historical:
Micah of Moresheth prophesied in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, Micah 1:1, which puts him in the second half of the eighth century before Christ, while Assyria was swallowing the northern kingdom and pressing on Judah. He came from a small country town, and the first target of his charge is the capital's governing class, the 'leaders of Jacob' and 'rulers of the house of Israel.' These were the judges, elders and officials who sat in the gate and decided cases, which is why 'justice' is the word they are charged with knowing.

An eighth-century prophet could expect to be paid. Seers and diviners were part of the royal and civic furniture, consulted for a fee, and the temptation to tailor an oracle to the purse was constant. Micah's charge in verse 5 is that the prophets treat their gift as a trade, blessing the people who feed them and declaring a holy war against those who do not.

The confident slogan of verse 11, 'Is not the LORD among us?', belongs to the Zion tradition, the conviction that the LORD had chosen Jerusalem and would defend it. That belief was sound as theology and ruinous as an insurance policy. A century later Jeremiah met the same slogan in the temple gate, Jeremiah 7:4. The elders in Jeremiah 26:17 to 19 then quote verse 12 word for word and recall that Hezekiah did not kill Micah but feared the LORD and sought His favor, so that the disaster was held back.
context.canonical:
Verse 12 has the unusual distinction of being quoted by another prophetic book as a precedent. In Jeremiah 26:18 the elders cite it, with the formula 'Micah the Moreshite prophesied,' to save Jeremiah's life, arguing that a prophet who announced the ruin of the temple had once been heeded and not executed. The sentence that sounded like blasphemy to the establishment is treated, a century on, as the mark of a true prophet.

The charges are not Micah's alone. Isaiah describes rulers who love bribes and ignore the widow, Isaiah 1:23, Zephaniah calls Jerusalem's princes roaring lions and her judges evening wolves, Zephaniah 3:3 and 4, and Malachi remembers the priesthood as a covenant betrayed, Malachi 2:7 to 8. Ezekiel 34:2 to 4 gives the fullest form of the shepherd indictment, charging Israel's shepherds with eating the fat and wearing the wool while the flock goes unfed.

The New Testament picks up all three themes. Jesus quotes Jeremiah's temple sermon when He clears the court, Mark 11:17, and wept over the city whose stones He said would be thrown down, Luke 19:41 to 44. He draws the shepherd contrast with the hired hand, John 10:11 to 13, and the apostles warn the elders of the church against greed and lording it over the flock, 1 Peter 5:2 to 3.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Micah did not write to inform the leaders of Jerusalem of their sins; they knew the law well enough. He wrote so that the people they were crushing would hear what the LORD thought of it, and so that anyone who held authority would be warned that proximity to the sacred buys no protection. The aim of the first panel is to remove excuses: justice is the one thing rulers are expected to know, and they have trained themselves to hate it.

The middle panel gives the hearer a way to tell true voices from false ones. A prophet who tilts his message according to who feeds him has disqualified himself, and Micah's own commission in verse 8 supplies the opposite pattern, a message that is powerful, just and costly. The last panel dismantles the comfort of verse 11. The people may keep saying 'Is not the LORD among us?', but Micah wanted them to see that the answer is yes, and that this is the problem. He also meant the sentence of verse 12 to be believed as a real possibility, which is why it could later be remembered as the moment Hezekiah turned. The word of judgment was given in order to be heeded.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what Micah said to specific leaders in a specific crisis, and the cannibal imagery is rhetoric, not a report of what happened in the gate. Nothing here commands a reader to treat every minister, magistrate or employer as an enemy. What the text does prescribe, by showing its opposite, is the shape of faithful leadership: knowing justice, speaking without a price tag, and refusing to hide behind a sacred address.

The application is sharpest for anyone who handles other people's trust, whether as pastor, official, teacher or employer. Verse 11 is a mirror for religious communities in particular: God's presence among His people is never a guarantee of His approval. It is also worth noting that Micah says nothing against the offices themselves. The cure for the shepherds' failure in the rest of the book is not no shepherd, but a better one.

debates.question: Was the destruction of Jerusalem in verse 12 fulfilled, given that Hezekiah's Jerusalem survived Assyria?

views.label: Averted for a generation, then fulfilled later
views.case: Jeremiah 26:19 says Hezekiah feared the LORD and sought His favor and the LORD relented of the disaster He had pronounced, so Jerusalem was spared in that generation. The same fate fell when Babylon destroyed the city and temple in 586 BC, and Jesus' words over the temple in Luke 19:44 repeat the pattern once more.

views.label: A conditional prophetic threat
views.case: The oracle functions as a genuine but conditional warning: the leaders' sin deserves such judgment, and God is free to relent upon repentance, as He did, without the word failing. Jeremiah 18:7 to 8 states the principle that an announced disaster can be withdrawn if the nation turns.

debates.bearing: Both views uphold the truthfulness of prophecy: God's warnings aim at repentance, and mercy in response to repentance is not a broken promise but the very heart of God.

debates.question: How can a hearer tell a true prophet from a false one, since both claim the name of the LORD?

views.label: By the test of fulfillment
views.case: Deuteronomy 18:21 to 22 says that when a prophet speaks in the LORD's name and the word does not come true, the LORD has not spoken it. On this view the false prophets of verse 5, who promise peace, are exposed when the peace does not come, and Micah is vindicated when the judgment does.

views.label: By the content and character of the message
views.case: Fulfillment can only be seen afterward, while the people must decide now. Micah gives marks that can be read in the present: the false prophets tailor their message to what they are paid, verse 5 and verse 11, while the true prophet declares sin, verse 8. Jeremiah 7:4 likewise condemns trust in a comforting slogan.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Deuteronomy itself pairs the test of outcome with a test of loyalty to the LORD, Deuteronomy 13:1 to 3, so neither stands alone. Careful readers hold the two together, since a message that flatters power and pays its prophet is suspect from the start, even before time tests it.

debates.bearing: The passage teaches suspicion toward any message whose content happens to match its income, and patience toward the prophet who tells a costly truth. It does not make popularity or unpopularity a proof either way.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 asks whether the rulers should not know mishpat, a word whose root sense is a decision given in a case, then the right ordering that such decisions protect. The question assumes they knew the standard and chose otherwise, and verse 2 gives the ugly inversion, hating good and loving evil, a reversal of the call in Amos 5:15 to hate evil and love good and establish justice in the gate.

The butchery verbs of verses 2 and 3 are chosen to disgust. 'Tear' and 'strip' are what a flayer does, the bones are broken, and the final clause compares the people to meat chopped for a pot. The point is not the gore but the intimacy: the leaders do not stand at a distance from the people they harm, they sit down to eat them.

Verse 4 says the LORD will 'hide His face.' That is the language of covenant curse, as in Deuteronomy 31:17, where God warns that He will abandon the people and hide His face when they forsake Him. Silence is the sentence. The same logic stands behind the closing line of verse 7, 'no answer from God', and recalls Saul's fate, 1 Samuel 28:6, where the LORD did not answer by dreams or Urim or prophets.

In verse 5 the prophets 'chew with their teeth', a verb of biting that makes the mouth of the prophet a mouth that feeds and bites, peace for those who fill it and war on those who do not. The 'cover their mouths' of verse 7 is a gesture of shame and mourning; Leviticus 13:45 prescribes it for a person with a skin disease, who must cover the face below the eyes and cry out. The seers are made to look like outcasts.

Verse 8 is the moral center. Micah says he is full of power, 'with the Spirit of the LORD, with justice and courage.' The three nouns stand side by side: the Spirit supplies the power, and the power is aimed at justice and courage in speaking. The goal is also named exactly, to declare to Jacob his transgression, a phrase that echoes the opening of the book, Micah 1:5. A prophet's gift is not a private blessing but a commission to say what no one wants to hear.

In verse 12 the 'wooded ridge' is literally 'high places of a forest,' the temple mount reduced to scrub. 'Heap of rubble' uses a word for ruins that Psalm 79:1 applies to Jerusalem after an invasion, so Micah's hearers would have recognised it as the language of a city already mourned.

typology.type: The shepherds who devour the flock, Micah 3:1 to 3
typology.fulfillment: The picture of rulers who eat the flock they were set to feed is drawn out in Ezekiel 34:2 to 4, where the shepherds eat the fat and do not strengthen the weak. Jesus contrasts the hired hand with 'the good shepherd,' who 'lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11 to 12. Where the false shepherd is nourished by the flock, the true Shepherd nourishes the flock with Himself. The type falls short in that earthly shepherds are only more or less faithful; Christ is the only one who is wholly what a shepherd should be, and He is the pattern by which every pastor is judged, 1 Peter 5:2 to 4.

typology.type: The Spirit-filled prophet who declares sin, Micah 3:8
typology.fulfillment: Micah's claim to be full of power by the Spirit of the LORD is a pointer to the One on whom the Spirit rests without measure. Jesus reads Isaiah 61 in Nazareth and says, 'The Spirit of the Lord is on Me,' Luke 4:18, and then meets the same hostility Micah expected. The correspondence is real, but the escalation matters: Micah receives the Spirit for a task, while Jesus is the Word made flesh who gives the Spirit, John 1:33. The type also points forward to the church, who after prayer are 'filled with the Holy Spirit' and speak God's word boldly, Acts 4:31.

typology.type: The temple mount reduced to a field, Micah 3:12
typology.fulfillment: The sentence on the sanctuary is repeated in Jesus' words, 'not one stone here will be left on another,' Matthew 24:2, and in His weeping over the city in Luke 19:41 to 44. When the temple was challenged, He pointed to Himself: 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again,' John 2:19. The pattern is judgment, then something new raised in its place. The type falls short where the temple was a building; the true dwelling of God is a person and then the people joined to Him, Ephesians 2:21 to 22.

study.christ:
Micah 3 is a dark chapter, but its darkness is the kind that makes a light easy to see. Every failure in it is a failure of office, and each office finds its fulfilment in Christ.

The rulers who devour the people are answered by the King who gives Himself to be eaten, as Jesus says at the Supper, 'Take and eat; this is My body,' Matthew 26:26. Where Micah's rulers tore flesh from the bones of the poor, Christ offers His own flesh for the life of the world, John 6:51. The same imagery is turned inside out: an exploiter takes life from the people, the Shepherd gives life to them.

The prophets who preach for hire are answered by the Prophet who spoke the truth without a price. Jesus says that He came to proclaim good news to the poor, Luke 4:18, and when it cost Him His life He did not soften what He said. Like Micah, He stood against an establishment whose chief priests and scribes looked for a way to kill Him, Mark 11:18, and He named the fruit of their practice, Matthew 23:23, that they had neglected justice, mercy and faithfulness. Micah's lonely 'but as for me' in verse 8 has its full realization in the One who was not merely filled with the Spirit for a moment but anointed with it without measure.

The priests who teach for a price are answered by the great High Priest who 'through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God,' Hebrews 9:14, and who gives access freely. The temple mount that Micah says will be reduced to a field is answered by the temple of His body, which was destroyed and raised, John 2:19 to 21, and by the people who are now 'being built together' into a dwelling for God, Ephesians 2:22.

There is also the matter of the people Micah calls 'My people.' The God who says that phrase over the exploited is the God who in Christ comes to the poor and bears their wounds. He wept over the city Micah condemned, and His tears are the exact opposite of the leaders' indifference.

A caution keeps this honest. Micah 3 does not predict Christ by name, and the chapter's own subject is the leaders' sin and Jerusalem's fall. The Christ-ward line runs through what the passage shows is missing, a Shepherd, a Prophet and a Priest who are what these were not, and through the New Testament's own use of the temple sentence.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows about God is how closely He binds Himself to the powerless. He calls the exploited 'my people' in verses 3 and 5, and what is done to them is treated as done to Him. Justice is not an abstract ideal in this passage; it is the form God's care takes when it meets the strong. The question 'Should you not know justice?' presumes that God Himself has made justice knowable and that those with power are accountable to Him for it.

The chapter also shows a God who cannot be bought, and whose words cannot be bought on His behalf. The prophets' trade works only if God can be induced to bless the people who pay. Micah says He cannot be: the vision fails, the night falls, the diviners are left with nothing to say. A God who could be hired would be an idol.

It shows God's judgment as something that answers a sin in kind and that begins at His own house. The leaders who gave no hearing to the poor cry out and are given no hearing, verse 4. The prophets who spoke for pay lose every oracle. The city built on bloodshed is taken apart, and the sanctuary is not exempt. Peter later says that judgment begins with the family of God, 1 Peter 4:17, and Micah is an early witness. The word in verse 11, 'Is not the LORD among us?', is true, and the truth cuts the other way: a God who is present is a God who sees.

Yet the chapter shows His patience as well. By Jeremiah 26:19 we learn that this very threat moved Hezekiah to fear the LORD and seek His favor, and the LORD relented. Judgment announced is judgment that can be turned aside, and the announcement itself is mercy.

Finally, the chapter shows God as the one who gives and equips the true messenger. The Spirit's power, justice and courage in verse 8 are His gifts, not Micah's qualities. Worship here starts from the recognition that the same God who hides His face from fraud opens His mouth through a faithful witness, and the right response is not to defend our religious address but to pray for ears to hear.

crossReferences.note: Elders quote Micah 3:12 as a precedent. Hezekiah did not execute Micah; he feared the LORD and sought His favor, and the LORD relented. It shows that Micah's sentence was heard as a call to repentance and that a true prophet's word can be remembered a hundred years later as the pattern to follow.

The fullest form of the shepherd charge. The shepherds eat the fat, wear the wool and butcher the sheep, and they do not strengthen the weak or search for the lost. It gives the positive duties of a shepherd that Micah's rulers neglect, and it leads to the promise that the LORD Himself will shepherd the flock.

Jeremiah meets the same slogan Micah heard in verse 11. The people chant 'the temple of the LORD' as a charm against disaster while stealing, murdering and swearing falsely. The pair of texts shows that trust in sacred space without obedience was a persistent trap in Judah, not a one-time lapse.

Habakkuk's woe on the one who builds a city with bloodshed is close to Micah 3:10, where the leaders build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with iniquity. The echo shows a shared prophetic conviction that a city founded on violence cannot stand, however sacred its name.

The root of the hidden face in verse 4. God warns that when the people forsake the covenant He will hide His face from them, so that troubles come and they ask whether their God is no longer with them. Micah applies the curse to leaders who cry out to the LORD while still doing evil.

A famine of hearing the words of the LORD is the larger version of the silence in Micah 3:6 and 7. Micah's contemporary describes people staggering about seeking the word and not finding it. It shows that the loss of the word is itself a judgment, not only a consequence.

Malachi remembers what a priest should be: his lips preserve knowledge, and he is the messenger of the LORD of Hosts. Micah 3:11 shows the priests teaching for a price. The two passages frame the priesthood's failure from beginning to end of the prophets, a vocation emptied by profit.

Jesus warns of false prophets who look like sheep and are ravenous wolves inside. Micah's prophets who proclaim peace for those who feed them are exactly that, and the warning passes the test of Micah 3 to the church: judge teachers by what drives them, and by whether they bite those who do not pay.

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem and says its enemies will level it, leaving no stone on another, because it did not recognise the time of its visitation. The pronouncement matches Micah 3:12, but the tone has changed: where Micah thunders, Jesus weeps, and the verdict is delivered by the one who has come to save.

When asked for a sign, Jesus points to the temple of His body, to be destroyed and raised in three days. The leveled mount of Micah 3:12 meets its answer in the new temple that death cannot hold, and the reason for hope for the sanctuary is no longer a building but a person.

Peter charges elders to shepherd God's flock not for greed but with eagerness, not lording it over those entrusted to them. It reads like a positive version of Micah 3:11, and it shows the apostolic church taking the prophets' indictment as its own pastoral standard.

After prayer the believers are filled with the Holy Spirit and speak the word of God boldly. Micah's lonely 'filled with power by the Spirit' in verse 8 becomes the shared condition of a whole community, in fulfilment of the promise that the Spirit would be poured out on all, Joel 2:28.

study.oneStory:
Chapter 3 sits at the center of a pattern the Bible tells again and again. God gives His people leaders, kings to judge, priests to teach and prophets to speak, and the leaders turn the gift into a means of feeding themselves. The pattern starts early, with Eli's sons who took the best of the offerings and ended with their father's house in ruin, 1 Samuel 2:12 to 17, and it runs through the kings of Israel and Judah until the exile.

In the larger story Micah 3 answers a question left by creation. Human beings were made to rule on God's behalf, Genesis 1:26 to 28, and to guard the garden, Genesis 2:15. When rule is exercised for appetite instead of service, the guardians turn predators. The cannibal picture of verses 2 and 3 is the image of dominion turned inside out.

The chapter also looks forward. Its last verse removes the sanctuary that gave the false leaders their confidence, and in the next chapter that same mountain is lifted up above the hills, Micah 4:1. Judgment on the leaders makes room for a different kind of ruler, the Bethlehem shepherd of 5:2 to 4, who stands and shepherds in the strength of the LORD.

The Gospels show how heavily Micah 3 weighs on the story of Jesus. The establishment that rejects Him is made of the same three offices, rulers, priests and prophets, and He meets them with the same verdict on the temple, Matthew 24:2. His cleansing of the temple and His weeping over Jerusalem are Micah 3 acted out. Yet where Micah's word ends in rubble, Jesus' word ends in resurrection, John 2:19.

The story ends in a city with no temple, because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. There the only Ruler is the Lamb, and His people reign with Him, Revelation 22:5, and there is no longer any curse, Revelation 22:3. What Micah 3 shows being destroyed is a sanctuary built on bloodshed, and what Revelation shows being built is a city where the throne of God and of the Lamb is within it, and His servants worship Him.

sermon.why: No focused expository sermon on Micah 3 by a trusted expositor could be verified by web search this session, so none is cited rather than risk misattribution.

quiz.q: How does Micah describe what the rulers do to the people (verses 2 to 3)?

options.text: As cannibalism: tearing off skin, breaking bones, and eating the flesh of the people.
options.note: Micah uses shocking butchery imagery to expose the horror of their oppression.

options.text: As gentle but misguided leadership.
options.note: The imagery is violent and damning, not a picture of well-meaning error.

options.text: As neglect, simply ignoring the people's needs.
options.note: The rulers do gravely fail the people, though the imagery shows active, violent exploitation, not mere neglect.

options.text: As heavy but lawful taxation.
options.note: The picture is of devouring the people, not merely taxing them.

quiz.q: What was wrong with the prophets in verse 5?

options.text: They proclaimed peace to those who fed them and war on those who did not, preaching for profit.
options.note: Their message was for sale, tailored to who paid them.

options.text: They preached too much judgment and frightened people.
options.note: Their fault was flattery for pay, not excessive warning.

options.text: They refused to prophesy at all.
options.note: They failed to give the true word of God, though rather than staying silent they prophesied falsely for pay.

options.text: They correctly warned of judgment but were ignored.
options.note: They were the false prophets; Micah is the one telling the truth.

quiz.q: How does Micah describe himself in verse 8?

options.text: Filled with power by the Spirit of the LORD, with justice and courage, to declare Israel's sin.
options.note: Micah is Spirit-empowered to speak the truth others sold or suppressed.

options.text: Reluctant and afraid to say anything unpopular.
options.note: He is marked by courage, not fear, in this verse.

options.text: Wealthy from the fees he charged for his prophecies.
options.note: That describes the false prophets; Micah stands against them.

options.text: One prophet among many who agreed with the leaders.
options.note: Micah is indeed a prophet, though he stands alone against the leaders rather than among those who agreed with them.

quiz.q: What false confidence did the leaders hold in verse 11?

options.text: That because the LORD was among them, no disaster could come, even while they took bribes.
options.note: They presumed God's presence guaranteed safety regardless of their sin.

options.text: That their army was strong enough to repel Assyria.
options.note: Trusting military strength was a real false confidence, though verse 11 names their presumption on the LORD's presence, not their army.

options.text: That they had repented and been forgiven.
options.note: They had not repented; they presumed on God while sinning.

options.text: That the surrounding nations were their allies.
options.note: Their false security was leaning on the LORD's presence, not alliances.

quiz.q: How does the failure of these leaders point to Christ?

options.text: It cries out for the true Shepherd, Prophet, and Priest, fulfilled in Jesus who serves, speaks truth, and gives Himself.
options.note: Christ is everything these corrupt leaders were not.

options.text: It shows that all leadership is hopeless and should be abolished.
options.note: The chapter does expose the deep failure of human leadership, though it points not to abolishing leadership but to longing for the true Leader, Christ.

options.text: It has no bearing on Christ or the gospel.
options.note: The failed shepherds set up the promise of the true Shepherd, Jesus.

options.text: It teaches that God will always protect the temple no matter what.
options.note: The opposite; the temple is leveled, and Christ becomes the true Temple.

questions: Micah says the leaders should know justice but instead despise it. Where has familiarity with God's word left you knowing what is right yet failing to do it?
The prophets shaped their message around who paid them. Are there people or pressures that quietly shape you to say only what others want to hear?
The leaders leaned on God's presence while ignoring His commands. Where might you be presuming on God's grace while resisting His call to change?
Micah stood alone, filled with the Spirit, to tell the truth. Is God calling you to speak a hard truth in love where it would be easier to stay silent?
Jesus is the Shepherd who was devoured for His sheep rather than devouring them. How does His self-giving leadership reshape the way you lead or serve others?

translationNotes.note: The contrast with 2:11 is deliberate: the false prophet is a man of wind, ruach, while Micah is filled with the ruach, the Spirit, of the LORD; the same Hebrew word carries opposite weight.
The leaders' slogan, Is not the LORD among us, echoes true covenant language but is here twisted into false security, presuming God's presence guarantees immunity from judgment.

This verse is quoted in Jeremiah 26:18, where the elders recall that Micah's warning led Hezekiah to seek the LORD, so the threatened destruction was postponed; a wooded ridge pictures the holy site returned to wild scrubland.
